claims.text: The initial NiFeCoCrPd alloy is produced by powder metallurgy.
The initial alloy is a single-phase FCC solid solution.
Minor Pd additions followed by aging at 500 °C trigger nanoscale precipitation in NiFeCoCrPd.
The resulting precipitates are uniformly distributed, FCC, and smaller than 50 nm.
The nanoscale precipitates act as crack-bridging agents.
Crack deflection and bridging provide crack-tip shielding that impedes crack propagation.
Controlled precipitation modifies local stress fields and energy-dissipation pathways.
The precipitation-mediated shielding retains or enhances toughness.
Optimally aged alloys containing 5–10 at% Pd will have more than 10% higher fracture toughness than the as-cast or non-aged baseline.
Over-aging that coarsens precipitates beyond 50 nm will decrease toughness.
Excessive Pd can alter the matrix phase and invalidate the proposed mechanism.
The proposed mechanism applies while precipitates remain uniformly distributed below 50 nm and the matrix remains FCC.
The general mechanism linking nanoscale precipitates to enhanced toughness is established.
The optimal Pd content, aging duration, and magnitude of toughness improvement may vary with processing nuances.
The experiment will compare 0, 5, and 10 at% Pd and aging durations of 1–4 hours at 500 °C.
Failure to obtain greater than 10% toughness improvement, or failure to observe the predicted association between sub-50 nm precipitates and toughness, is designated as falsifying the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The investigated samples are specified as powder-metallurgy products, but the baseline is ambiguously described as either as-cast or non-aged. An as-cast baseline differs in processing route as well as aging state and therefore is not a controlled counterpart to the stated initial material.
